notes.definition: Genetic engineering is a process which involves modifying the genome of an organism by introducing a gene from another organism to give a desired characteristic.
explanation: Every organism's genome is its entire genetic material. In genetic engineering, scientists take a gene that codes for a useful characteristic from one organism and put it into the genome of another organism, often of a completely different species. The organism that receives the gene can then make the protein the gene codes for, so it shows the new, desired characteristic. Organisms modified in this way are called genetically modified (GM) organisms.

Bacterial cells have been genetically engineered to produce useful substances. The most important example is human insulin, used to treat people with diabetes. The human gene for insulin is put into bacteria, which are grown in large vessels and make human insulin that can be collected and purified. Before this, insulin was extracted from the pancreases of pigs and cattle. Plant crops have also been genetically engineered, for example to be resistant to diseases or to produce bigger, better fruits.

Crops that have had their genes modified are called genetically modified (GM) crops. GM crops include ones that are resistant to insect attack, because they produce a substance that is toxic to insect pests, and ones that are resistant to herbicides (weedkillers), so farmers can spray fields to kill weeds without harming the crop. GM crops generally show increased yields, because less of the crop is lost to pests, weeds and disease. Modern medical research is also exploring the possibility of genetic modification to overcome some inherited disorders, for example by inserting a working copy of a faulty gene into a patient's cells (gene therapy).

Genetic engineering has potential benefits in agriculture and medicine: higher crop yields to feed a growing population, crops that need fewer pesticides, crops with added nutrients, and medicines such as insulin made cheaply and in large amounts. There are also potential risks. Concerns about GM crops include the effect on populations of wild flowers and insects: for example, genes for herbicide resistance could spread to wild relatives by pollen, and insect-resistant crops could harm insects that are not pests. Some people feel the effects of eating GM crops on human health have not been fully explored.

Some people have objections to genetic engineering for ethical or religious reasons. They may feel it is wrong to move genes between species, worry about where the technology could lead (for example, to choosing characteristics in human babies), or think it is unfair that large companies own and control GM seeds. In the exam you need to be able to explain both the potential benefits and the risks of genetic engineering in agriculture and in medicine, and give reasons why some people object.
keyFacts: Genetic engineering modifies the genome of an organism by introducing a gene from another organism.
The aim is to give the organism a desired characteristic.
Bacteria have been genetically engineered to produce human insulin to treat diabetes.
Plant crops have been engineered to resist diseases or to produce bigger, better fruits.
Crops with modified genes are called genetically modified (GM) crops.
GM crops include ones resistant to insect attack or to herbicides.
GM crops generally show increased yields.
Concerns include effects on wild flower and insect populations, and on human health.
Medical research is exploring genetic modification to overcome some inherited disorders.

keyTerms.definition: Modifying the genome of an organism by introducing a gene from another organism to give a desired characteristic.
The entire genetic material of an organism.
A crop plant whose genes have been modified by genetic engineering, for example to resist insects or herbicides.
A chemical that kills plants, used as a weedkiller.
Something used to carry a gene into a cell, usually a bacterial plasmid or a virus (Higher tier).
A small ring of DNA found in bacteria, often used as a vector in genetic engineering.
Using genetic modification to try to overcome an inherited disorder by giving cells a working copy of a gene.

workedExamples.title: Explaining how a GM crop increases yield
workedExamples.question: A farmer grows a variety of maize that has been genetically modified to resist herbicides. Explain how this could increase her yield.
steps: The farmer can spray the whole field with herbicide.
The herbicide kills the weeds but not the GM maize.
With fewer weeds, there is less competition for light, water and mineral ions.
So the maize grows better and the yield increases.
workedExamples.answer: Weeds can be killed without harming the crop, reducing competition, so more maize is produced.

workedExamples.title: Calculating a percentage increase in yield
workedExamples.question: A conventional cotton crop yields 1.6 tonnes per hectare. An insect-resistant GM cotton crop grown nearby yields 2.0 tonnes per hectare. Calculate the percentage increase.

workedExamples.title: Main steps of genetic engineering (Higher tier)
workedExamples.question: Describe how bacteria are genetically engineered to make human insulin.
steps: Enzymes are used to cut out (isolate) the human insulin gene from human DNA.
The gene is inserted into a vector, here a bacterial plasmid.
The plasmid is used to carry the gene into bacterial cells.
The bacteria multiply, and every new bacterium contains the gene and makes human insulin.
workedExamples.answer: Isolate gene with enzymes, insert into plasmid vector, put plasmid into bacteria, grow bacteria to produce insulin.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think genetic engineering and selective breeding are the same.
misconceptions.right: In fact selective breeding uses existing variation within a species over many generations, while genetic engineering directly introduces a gene from another organism, often a different species.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the bacteria used to make insulin are human cells or contain the whole human genome.
misconceptions.right: In fact only one human gene, the insulin gene, is inserted into each bacterium.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think herbicide-resistant crops are resistant to insects.
misconceptions.right: In fact herbicide resistance means the crop is not killed by weedkiller. Insect resistance is a different modification, where the crop produces a substance toxic to insect pests.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often state as fact that GM food is harmful to eat.
misconceptions.right: In fact the specification says some people feel the effects on human health have not been fully explored. That is a concern, not a proven harm.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the gene is added to an adult plant or animal.
misconceptions.right: In fact genes are transferred at an early stage of development so that the organism develops with the desired characteristic (Higher tier).

realWorld: Almost all the insulin used by people with diabetes today is human insulin made by genetically engineered bacteria or yeast.
Golden Rice has been genetically modified to produce beta-carotene, which the body uses to make vitamin A, to help reduce vitamin A deficiency.
Bt cotton and Bt maize contain a bacterial gene that makes a protein toxic to certain insect pests, reducing crop losses and pesticide spraying.
Gene therapy trials are testing whether inserting working copies of genes can treat inherited disorders such as cystic fibrosis.
higherTier: The main steps in the process of genetic engineering: (1) enzymes are used to isolate (cut out) the required gene; (2) this gene is inserted into a vector, usually a bacterial plasmid or a virus; (3) the vector is used to insert the gene into the required cells; (4) genes are transferred to the cells of animals, plants or microorganisms at an early stage in their development so that they develop with the desired characteristics.

The enzymes that cut DNA are often called restriction enzymes, and an enzyme called ligase joins the gene into the cut plasmid. Using the same cutting enzyme on the gene and the plasmid leaves matching ends that join together.
Transferring a gene at an early stage (for example into an embryo, a fertilised egg, or a plant cell that will grow into a whole plant) means every cell of the adult organism contains the new gene.
examTips: Learn the definition word for word: modifying the genome of an organism by introducing a gene from another organism to give a desired characteristic.
For benefits and risks questions, give both sides and use specific examples (insulin, insect-resistant crops, herbicide-resistant crops).
Higher tier: describe the steps in order: enzymes isolate gene, insert into vector (plasmid or virus), vector inserts gene into cells, done at an early stage of development.
Do not just write 'GM food is dangerous'. Write that some people feel the effects on human health have not been fully explored.
When explaining how herbicide-resistant crops increase yield, link it to killing weeds, which reduces competition for light, water and minerals.
summary: Genetic engineering introduces a gene from another organism to give a desired characteristic.
Bacteria are engineered to make human insulin for people with diabetes.
GM crops can resist insects, herbicides or disease, or have bigger, better fruits, and generally give higher yields.
Concerns: effects on wild flowers and insects, and effects on human health not fully explored.
Research is exploring genetic modification to treat inherited disorders.
Higher: enzymes isolate the gene, which goes into a vector (plasmid or virus) that inserts it into cells at an early stage of development.

questions.question: Which is the best definition of genetic engineering?
options: Breeding plants with desired characteristics over many generations
Producing genetically identical copies of an organism
Modifying the genome of an organism by introducing a gene from another organism
Changing an organism's environment to change its phenotype
markScheme: 1 mark: modifying the genome of an organism by introducing a gene from another organism
questions.explanation: Genetic engineering moves a gene from one organism to another. Breeding over generations is selective breeding, and identical copies are clones.

questions.question: Which substance is made by genetically engineered bacteria to treat diabetes?
markScheme: 1 mark: human insulin
questions.explanation: The human insulin gene is put into bacteria, which then produce human insulin. Penicillin is an antibiotic made by a mould, not by engineered bacteria.

questions.question: What does the abbreviation GM stand for?
markScheme: 1 mark: genetically modified
questions.explanation: Crops whose genes have been modified by genetic engineering are called genetically modified (GM) crops.

questions.question: A crop plant has been genetically modified to be resistant to herbicides. What does this mean?
options: The crop cannot catch any diseases
The crop is not killed when sprayed with weedkiller
markScheme: 1 mark: the crop is not killed by weedkiller
questions.explanation: Herbicides are weedkillers. A herbicide-resistant crop survives spraying, while weeds are killed. Insect resistance is a different modification.

questions.question: Which is a concern about growing GM crops that is stated in the AQA specification?
options: GM crops always have lower yields
Effects on populations of wild flowers and insects
markScheme: 1 mark: effects on populations of wild flowers and insects
questions.explanation: Concerns include effects on wild flowers and insects and on human health. GM crops generally show increased yields and often need less pesticide.

questions.question: How does an insect-resistant GM crop usually lead to increased yield?
options: Less of the crop is damaged or eaten by insect pests
The crop photosynthesises faster at night
The crop no longer needs water
markScheme: 1 mark: less of the crop is damaged or eaten by insect pests
questions.explanation: Insect-resistant crops produce a substance toxic to insect pests, so less of the crop is lost and the yield rises.

questions.question: What is the main difference between genetic engineering and selective breeding?
options: Selective breeding is faster than genetic engineering
Genetic engineering can introduce a gene from a different species
Selective breeding introduces new genes from bacteria
Genetic engineering only works in animals
markScheme: 1 mark: genetic engineering can introduce a gene from a different species
questions.explanation: Genetic engineering transfers specific genes between organisms, even between species, and is faster. Selective breeding works within a species using existing variation over many generations.

questions.question: (Higher) What is used to isolate the required gene in genetic engineering?
markScheme: 1 mark: enzymes
questions.explanation: Enzymes are used to cut out (isolate) the required gene from the DNA. Antibodies, hormones and antibiotics do not cut DNA.

questions.question: (Higher) Which of these is usually used as a vector in genetic engineering?
markScheme: 1 mark: a bacterial plasmid
questions.explanation: Vectors carry the gene into cells. The usual vectors are bacterial plasmids or viruses. Red blood cells have no nucleus and could not do this.

questions.question: (Higher) Why are genes transferred into animal or plant cells at an early stage in their development?
options: So that the organism develops with the desired characteristic in all its cells
Because adult cells have no DNA
To stop the organism from reproducing
So that the gene is removed before adulthood
markScheme: 1 mark: so the organism develops with the desired characteristic (in all its cells)
questions.explanation: If the gene is added at an early stage, for example to an embryo, it is copied into every cell as the organism develops. Adult cells do contain DNA.

questions.question: A farm grew a GM maize crop that yielded 9 tonnes per hectare, compared with 7 tonnes per hectare from a non-GM crop. Calculate the difference in yield.
markScheme: 1 mark: 2 (tonnes per hectare)
questions.explanation: 9 − 7 = 2 tonnes per hectare.

questions.question: A non-GM soya crop yields 2.5 tonnes per hectare. A GM soya crop yields 3.0 tonnes per hectare. Calculate the percentage increase in yield.
markScheme: 1 mark: increase = 0.5 tonnes per hectare
questions.explanation: Increase = 3.0 − 2.5 = 0.5. Percentage increase = 0.5 ÷ 2.5 × 100 = 20%.

questions.question: A farmer grows conventional cotton and loses 30% of a potential 2000 kg crop to insect pests. With insect-resistant GM cotton she loses only 5%. Calculate how many more kilograms of cotton she harvests with the GM crop.
markScheme: 1 mark: conventional harvest = 2000 × 0.70 = 1400 kg; GM harvest = 2000 × 0.95 = 1900 kg
1 mark: difference = 500 kg
questions.explanation: Conventional: 70% of 2000 = 1400 kg. GM: 95% of 2000 = 1900 kg. Difference = 500 kg (or 25% of 2000 kg).

questions.question: A population of genetically engineered bacteria doubles every 20 minutes. Starting with 1 bacterium, how many bacteria containing the insulin gene will there be after 3 hours, assuming ideal conditions?
markScheme: 1 mark: number of divisions = 180 ÷ 20 = 9
1 mark: 2⁹ = 512
questions.explanation: 3 hours = 180 minutes, so there are 180 ÷ 20 = 9 doublings. 1 × 2⁹ = 512. Every new cell contains the plasmid with the insulin gene.

questions.question: Give one characteristic that crop plants have been genetically engineered to have.
markScheme: 1 mark: any one, e.g. resistance to disease, insect attack or herbicides; bigger, better fruits
questions.explanation: Crops have been modified to resist diseases, insects or herbicides, or to produce bigger, better fruits.

questions.question: Name the disease treated with human insulin made by genetically engineered bacteria.
markScheme: 1 mark: diabetes
questions.explanation: People with diabetes (especially type 1) need insulin injections; genetically engineered bacteria provide a reliable supply of human insulin.

questions.question: Give one reason why some people worry about eating GM crops.
acceptedAnswers: effects on human health not fully explored
markScheme: 1 mark: the effects on human health have not been fully explored / are unknown
questions.explanation: Some people feel that the long-term effects of eating GM crops on human health have not been fully investigated.

questions.question: Explain how growing a herbicide-resistant GM crop can increase yield.
acceptedAnswers: more light water minerals for crop
markScheme: 1 mark: the field can be sprayed with herbicide to kill weeds without killing the crop
1 mark: so there is less competition (for light, water, mineral ions), so the crop grows better
questions.explanation: The benefit comes from removing weeds, which compete with the crop for resources.

questions.question: Suggest two advantages of producing human insulin using genetically engineered bacteria rather than extracting insulin from animals.
acceptedAnswers: acceptable to vegetarians or religious groups
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two, e.g. can be made in large amounts quickly; cheaper; it is identical to human insulin so fewer reactions; no animals needed; acceptable to people with ethical or religious objections to animal products (max 2)
questions.explanation: Bacteria multiply quickly in fermenters, giving a large, reliable supply of insulin identical to that made by the human pancreas.

questions.question: Explain how growing insect-resistant GM crops could affect populations of insects that are not pests.
markScheme: 1 mark: the substance toxic to pests may also harm/kill other insects (e.g. pollinators that feed on pollen)
1 mark: reducing insect populations, which could affect food chains (animals that eat insects)
questions.explanation: This is one of the concerns about GM crops: effects on wider insect populations and the organisms that depend on them.

questions.question: Give two reasons why some people object to genetic engineering.
acceptedAnswers: wrong to move genes between species
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two, e.g. ethical or religious belief that it is wrong to interfere with genes or move them between species; could lead to designer babies; effects on health not fully explored; effects on wild flowers and insects; large companies control seed supplies (max 2)
questions.explanation: Objections can be ethical, religious, environmental or economic.

questions.question: (Higher) Describe the main steps used to genetically engineer bacteria to produce human insulin.
markScheme: 1 mark: enzymes are used to isolate (cut out) the human insulin gene
1 mark: the gene is inserted into a vector (a bacterial plasmid)
1 mark: the plasmid (vector) is put into bacteria, which multiply and produce insulin
questions.explanation: The sequence is: isolate the gene with enzymes, insert into a vector, use the vector to get the gene into bacterial cells, then grow the bacteria.

questions.question: (Higher) Name two types of vector used in genetic engineering and state the job of a vector.
markScheme: 1 mark: (bacterial) plasmid and virus (both needed)
1 mark: the vector carries/inserts the gene into the required cells
questions.explanation: Vectors are carriers. Plasmids are small rings of DNA in bacteria; viruses naturally insert their genetic material into cells.

questions.question: Genes for herbicide resistance might spread from GM crops to wild plants. Explain how this could happen and why it could be a problem.
markScheme: 1 mark: pollen from the GM crop could fertilise (cross-pollinate) related wild plants/weeds
1 mark: the wild plants/weeds would then be resistant to herbicide
1 mark: so herbicides would no longer control these weeds / effect on wild flower populations
questions.explanation: This links to the concern about effects on wild flower populations: resistant 'superweeds' would be hard to control.

questions.question: Suggest how genetic modification might be used to overcome an inherited disorder such as cystic fibrosis, and give one difficulty.
acceptedAnswers: difficult to get into all cells
markScheme: 1 mark: insert a working (normal) copy of the gene into the patient's affected cells (using a vector such as a virus)
1 mark: difficulty, e.g. hard to get the gene into enough cells; effect may not last; possible side effects; still being researched
questions.explanation: This is gene therapy. Medical research is exploring it, but getting genes into the right cells safely is a major challenge.

questions.question: A government is deciding whether to allow farmers to grow GM crops. Give the arguments for and against.
markScheme: Indicative content. For: GM crops generally give increased yields; insect-resistant crops reduce losses and need less insecticide; herbicide-resistant crops let farmers control weeds easily; disease-resistant crops; bigger, better fruit or added nutrients; helps feed a growing population. Against: effects on populations of wild flowers (genes spreading by pollen) and insects (harm to non-pest insects); effects of eating GM crops on human health not fully explored; ethical or religious objections; control of seeds by large companies.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a balanced answer with at least two developed arguments on each side.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple arguments on one or both sides with little development.
questions.explanation: Evaluation questions reward balance: explain benefits with reasons, explain concerns with reasons, and avoid unsupported statements such as 'GM food is poison'.

questions.question:
(Higher) Scientists want to produce a crop plant that makes a substance toxic to insect pests. The gene for this substance is found in a species of bacterium.
Describe how genetic engineering could be used to produce this crop, and evaluate the use of such crops.
markScheme: Indicative content. Method: enzymes used to isolate (cut out) the gene from the bacterial DNA; gene inserted into a vector (plasmid or virus); vector used to insert the gene into plant cells; done at an early stage of development (e.g. cells that grow into whole plants) so all cells of the plant contain the gene; plants express the gene and make the toxin. Evaluation: benefits: resistant to insect attack, less crop lost, increased yields, fewer insecticide sprays needed; risks: toxin could harm non-pest insects such as pollinators, affecting insect populations; genes could spread to wild plants; effects on human health not fully explored; some people object for ethical reasons; a judgement or conclusion.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): describes the steps in a correct sequence and gives a balanced evaluation with benefits, risks and a conclusion.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes some of the steps and gives at least one benefit and one risk.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about inserting a gene or about benefits or risks.
questions.explanation: Top answers describe all four HT steps in order and then weigh up benefits against concerns, ending with a reasoned judgement.
